paragraphs: Hill-climbing search builds a solution by repeatedly choosing a promising nearby change. In inductive logic programming, this makes it possible to learn theories quickly, but it also creates short-sightedness: an immediately attractive step may hide a better sequence of changes. This paper investigates a way to give that search a longer view.

The authors integrate macro-operators into a hill-climbing learner. A macro packages multiple search steps into a larger move, allowing the learner to look ahead by a variable number of steps. This differs from always looking a fixed distance ahead or relying on templates to specify which longer moves should be considered.

Across several domains, the macro-based learner performs significantly better than the compared systems using fixed-depth look-ahead, template-based look-ahead, beam search, or determinate literals. The reported advantage is empirical. A further practical benefit is that the macros can be computed automatically, without user input or special domain properties such as determinacy.
icml-2004-a-comparative-study-on-methods.tldr: Automatically generated macro-operators improve a hill-climbing learner’s ability to look ahead and outperform several alternatives in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Nonnegative matrix factorization represents nonnegative observations through nonnegative components. This paper extends that idea to a multilayer generative network whose weights are also constrained to be nonnegative. The aim is to approximate the observed data while learning several levels of representation, with more complex structures expressed through simpler structures below them.

The proposed learning procedure updates weights by multiplication. A ratio describing the mismatch between the data and its approximation travels upward through the network, from the bottom layer to the top. Each layer uses this propagated information to adjust its weights, giving the method its name: multiplicative up-propagation.

The authors establish monotonic convergence for the algorithm, providing a theoretical result about its learning behavior. They also demonstrate the method on face images. The central contribution is the combination of a constrained multilayer model and an update procedure that can learn hierarchical representations, extending the representational role of ordinary nonnegative matrix factorization.
icml-2004-a-multiplicative-up-propagatio.tldr: Multiplicative up-propagation extends nonnegative matrix factorization to hierarchical representations with a demonstrated monotonic convergence property.

paragraphs: Supervised learning depends on labeled examples, but obtaining those labels can require substantial human effort. That burden becomes especially important when the requested answer is a complete ordering of alternatives rather than a single class. A ranking asks the annotator to supply relationships among multiple choices, making the labeling problem richer and potentially more expensive.

This paper generalizes pool-based active learning to label ranking. The central idea is to treat the selection of examples for labeling as part of the learning problem. Instead of taking the available training examples as fixed, the learner can choose from a pool when seeking additional ranking information.

The authors consider both pairwise decomposition and constraint classification as ways to represent ranking functions. Pairwise decomposition organizes the task around comparisons between alternatives, while constraint classification supplies another representation for the ordering problem. The contribution is a generalization of active learning that addresses these ranking representations and makes annotation effort an explicit concern in learning preferences.
icml-2004-active-learning-of-label-ranki.tldr: The paper extends pool-based active learning to learning complete rankings, addressing the cost of obtaining ranking labels.

paragraphs: Mixture estimation is an unsupervised learning problem in which a combination of probability distributions is fitted to observations. This paper studies maximum likelihood estimation when those distributions belong to exponential families. Its main contribution is a mathematical connection between this statistical fitting problem and a problem from information theory.

The authors prove that the mixture estimation problem is equivalent to a rate-distortion problem using Bregman divergences. Rate-distortion reasoning examines how much a representation can compress information while tolerating a specified kind of loss. Here, Bregman divergences provide the distortion measure that makes the connection to mixture estimation precise.

The paper also establishes new rate-distortion results for these divergences and analyzes the balance between compression and information preservation. Within that analysis, the information bottleneck method appears as a special case. This gives the work a unifying role: procedures described as fitting probabilistic mixtures and procedures described as compressing information can be studied through a shared mathematical formulation in the setting considered.
icml-2004-an-information-theoretic-analy.tldr: The paper proves an equivalence between exponential-family mixture estimation and rate-distortion optimization with Bregman divergences.

paragraphs: Choosing a learning algorithm would be easier if we could anticipate which kinds of problems it handles well. This paper takes a first step toward that goal by constructing a competence map: a description of regions of a problem landscape where a particular algorithm tends to succeed or fail on average.

The approach draws inspiration from the phase-transition perspective used in constraint satisfaction. Extensive, systematically organized experiments are used to map performance across problem instances. The emphasis is on identifying regions of behavior, so the result describes how an algorithm’s suitability changes across the studied landscape rather than reducing performance to a single overall assessment.

The authors illustrate the method with C4.5 and problems expressed in k-term DNF languages. They find a nontrivial region of failure and offer interpretations of the experimental results. This supports competence mapping as a way to expose structured weaknesses in a familiar algorithm, while keeping the conclusions tied to average behavior in the investigated problem family.
icml-2004-c4-5-competence-map-a-phase-tr.tldr: Systematic experiments map where C4.5 tends to succeed or fail and reveal a nontrivial failure region.

paragraphs: Multi-view learning uses unlabeled examples when attributes can be divided into independent, compatible subsets. Co-EM is one such approach and has outperformed co-training on many problems. Its requirements, however, constrain the underlying learner: it must estimate class probabilities and learn from examples whose labels are probabilistic rather than fixed.

This paper develops a way to use support vector machines within co-EM. The authors place linear classifiers in a probabilistic framework, allowing an SVM-based learner to meet those requirements. This extends co-EM beyond the naive Bayesian learners with which it had previously been studied and connects it to semi-supervised support vector learning.

Experiments compare semi-supervised support vector algorithms on text classification tasks under different conditions. These include conditions that violate the assumptions behind multi-view learning, making those assumptions part of the investigation. For some tasks, including course web page classification, the authors report the most accurate results available at the time, rather than claiming an advantage across every problem.
icml-2004-co-em-support-vector-learning-.tldr: A probabilistic formulation enables SVMs to participate in co-EM, with strong reported results on some text classification tasks.

paragraphs: Training many models creates a second learning problem: deciding which models should contribute to the final prediction system. This paper addresses that problem using libraries containing thousands of candidates. The library is built by varying both the learning algorithms and their parameter settings, creating a broad collection from which an ensemble can be assembled.

The proposed method uses forward stepwise selection. It grows the ensemble by adding models that maximize its performance at each selection step. The selection target is the performance of the combined ensemble, so the procedure focuses on what a candidate contributes to the developing collection.

A useful feature is that selection can target the metric relevant to the application, including accuracy, cross entropy, mean precision, or ROC area. The authors report experiments across seven test problems and ten metrics that demonstrate benefits from ensemble selection. The contribution is a practical way to turn a large, varied model library into an ensemble chosen for a specific evaluation objective.
icml-2004-ensemble-selection-from-librar.tldr: Forward stepwise selection builds ensembles from large model libraries while optimizing a chosen performance metric.

paragraphs: A classifier comparison can produce a different conclusion when the same data is randomized differently. This paper studies replicability in that specific sense: the probability that an experimental outcome repeats under another randomization. It treats the stability of the experimental conclusion as something that can be estimated and compared across evaluation procedures.

The authors present an unbiased estimator with the lowest variance among estimators formed as linear combinations of experimental outcomes on a given dataset. That qualification defines the scope of the optimality result. The estimator provides a principled tool for studying how reliably an experiment’s conclusion survives changes in data randomization.

Empirical comparisons show that both sampling schemes and hypothesis tests affect replicability. The results suggest avoiding sign tests because of low replicability; rank-sum tests perform better. Among the studied combinations, sorted-runs sampling with a t-test offers the most desirable balance of Type I error, Type II error, and replicability. These findings concern the evaluation procedure as well as the classifiers being evaluated.
icml-2004-estimating-replicability-of-cl.tldr: The paper estimates how reliably classifier experiments repeat and shows that sampling and hypothesis-test choices affect that reliability.

paragraphs: The application is assessing beef cattle as meat producers from measurements taken on live animals. The available experts judge animals relative to others in the same batch, so their assessments do not supply a single numerical target for each animal. The paper therefore frames the task as learning preferences from orderings of small groups.

The authors reduce this preference-learning problem to binary classification and use a support vector machine. They also select a subset of the available measurements, making feature selection part of the approach. The selection method builds on recursive feature elimination and adapts a metric-based model-selection method called ADJ.

The practical contribution is to align the learning task with the form of expertise actually available: relative judgments among animals. The feature-selection component addresses which measurements should support that learned ordering. The paper compares the resulting method with alternatives and discusses extension to more general settings, presenting the cattle assessment problem as a case study for a broader preference-learning approach.
icml-2004-feature-subset-selection-for-l.tldr: The paper combines SVM preference learning with recursive feature selection to learn experts’ relative assessments of beef cattle.

paragraphs: Some classification problems require a sequence of labels whose meanings depend on one another. When annotating or segmenting observations, predicting every label in isolation leaves out relationships between neighboring labels. This paper extends Gaussian process classification so that those dependencies become part of the prediction problem.

The approach predicts multiple labels while accounting for relationships between adjacent labels in a sequence. Its motivation is to preserve a rigorous probabilistic interpretation while addressing difficulties associated with parametric methods such as conditional random fields in high-dimensional input spaces. The contribution therefore connects Gaussian process classification with structured prediction, where the output consists of related decisions.

The authors evaluate the method on named entity recognition and pitch accent prediction. These experiments demonstrate that the approach is competitive on the studied tasks. The findings support the feasibility of using Gaussian processes for sequence annotation and segmentation while retaining label dependencies; they establish empirical competitiveness rather than a universal advantage over other sequence models.
icml-2004-gaussian-process-classificatio.tldr: Gaussian process classification is extended to dependent sequence labels and shows competitive results on two annotation tasks.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised clustering uses a small amount of labeled information to help organize otherwise unlabeled data. Existing approaches have used that information in two main ways: directing which groupings the clustering algorithm should prefer, or changing the distance function that determines which examples appear similar. This paper develops both approaches and brings them together.

Constraint-based guidance influences the grouping process itself. Metric learning changes the similarity relationships on which that process depends. The proposed algorithm integrates these two uses of supervision within a single principled framework, allowing the labeled information to shape both the grouping decisions and the underlying notion of distance.

The authors report that the unified approach produces better clusters in their experiments than either component used individually. It also outperforms previously proposed semi-supervised clustering algorithms in those comparisons. The result supports the value of combining direct guidance with a learned similarity measure: in the tested settings, the two sources of influence work better together than either does alone.
icml-2004-integrating-constraints-and-me.tldr: Combining clustering constraints with metric learning produces better clusters than either approach alone in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper estimates three-dimensional human body motion from silhouettes in video recorded by a single camera. It avoids requiring a detailed model of body shape and learns from real motion-capture data to support realistic motion estimates. The approach combines information about how a person is moving with information about their current outline.

A learned autoregressive dynamical model predicts the body’s state from its motion history. Automatically extracted silhouette descriptors supply visual evidence, and relevance vector machine regression combines the two. Among the combination methods studied, the most effective learns a nonlinear correction using both the predicted state and the observations together.

This correction matters because the tracker can use the new silhouette to update a motion-based prediction, rather than relying solely on either source of information. The authors demonstrate the approach with a full-body pose representation containing 54 parameters. They evaluate it quantitatively on motion-capture-based test sequences and qualitatively on a test video sequence.
icml-2004-learning-to-track-3d-human-mot.tldr: A sparse Bayesian tracker combines learned motion dynamics with silhouettes to estimate 3D body pose from single-camera video.

paragraphs: Clustering depends heavily on how distance is measured. In semi-supervised clustering, some background knowledge is available as pairs of examples that should be treated as similar or dissimilar. This paper uses those constraints to learn a distance representation, addressing the limitations of methods that apply one global linear transformation.

The proposed locally linear metric adaptation method uses transformations that are linear within local regions but nonlinear across the dataset as a whole. This gives the learned representation more flexibility than a single global linear change. The authors formulate the learning task as an optimization problem and present two methods for solving it.

Experiments on toy datasets show that the method can handle some difficult configurations that previous methods do not handle satisfactorily. Tests on real datasets also demonstrate its effectiveness. The findings support local adaptation as a useful way to express supervisory relationships when one global linear transformation is insufficient for the studied data, without establishing that it is preferable in every clustering setting.
icml-2004-locally-linear-metric-adaptati.tldr: Locally linear metric adaptation learns a globally nonlinear representation that handles some clustering cases poorly served by global linear methods.

paragraphs: A kernel-based classifier usually starts with one similarity function, but combining several kernels can be desirable. Learning the nonnegative combination weights for an SVM can be formulated as a convex optimization problem. The obstacle addressed here is computational: general-purpose solvers handle only relatively small problems, and the existing objective prevents direct use of efficient SVM optimization techniques.

The paper derives a new dual formulation as a second-order cone programming problem. It then uses Moreau-Yosida regularization to obtain a formulation compatible with sequential minimal optimization, or SMO. This connects the multiple-kernel learning problem to a technique important for large-scale SVM implementations.

The authors report that their SMO-based algorithm is significantly more efficient in experiments than the general-purpose interior-point methods available in the optimization toolboxes they compare against. The main advance is therefore an optimization reformulation that makes learning kernel combinations more computationally practical. The reported finding concerns solver efficiency, rather than a claim that combining kernels necessarily improves predictive accuracy.
icml-2004-multiple-kernel-learning-conic.tldr: A dual reformulation and regularization enable efficient SMO-based optimization for learning combinations of SVM kernels.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a family of nonparametric methods for binary classification with many input features. The classifier is constructed as a cascade of low-dimensional polynomial structures. This organizes the high-dimensional classification problem around a sequence of smaller polynomial components and forms the basis of the Polynomial MPMC Cascade algorithm.

Cascade construction uses Minimax Probability Machine Classification. This supplies direct estimates of classification accuracy and a stopping criterion that avoids expensive cross-validation measures. The construction time is linear in the input dimensionality and linear in the number of examples, making the approach potentially attractive when either quantity is large.

The reported experiments find the cascades competitive with leading classifiers, fast to compute, and not prone to overfitting in the evaluated settings. Their estimates of the maximum error rate on unseen data are generally accurate. Together, these results support the method as a potentially useful alternative to SVMs and standard MPMC, combining classification with an internal basis for estimating error and deciding when to stop construction.
icml-2004-nonparametric-classification-w.tldr: Polynomial MPMC cascades offer efficient high-dimensional classification with accuracy estimates and a stopping rule that avoids expensive cross-validation.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to remove redundant Boolean features, which record whether a property is present or absent. A feature is considered redundant when another feature or collection of features separates the classes better. The starting point is REDUCE, a method that compares features in pairs but was restricted to two-class problems in an inductive logic programming setting.

The authors improve that method and extend it to multiple classes through neighborhoods of examples. Each neighborhood contains examples from the same class that differ on relatively few features. A revised version of REDUCE is then applied to pairs of neighborhoods belonging to different classes.

This construction organizes the multiclass problem around comparisons between relatively similar groups within classes. Feature elimination is thereby tied to how those groups are distinguished across class boundaries. The authors analyze the method on a range of datasets. The central contribution is the neighborhood-based extension of redundancy elimination to multiclass data, together with an empirical examination of its performance.
icml-2004-redundant-feature-elimination-.tldr: The paper extends redundant Boolean feature elimination to multiple classes by comparing neighborhoods from different classes.

paragraphs: When labeled examples are scarce, a graph can connect both labeled and unlabeled examples according to their distances. A minimum-cut method assigns labels by partitioning that graph while respecting the known labels. This paper extends that approach by introducing randomness into the graph structure to address shortcomings of the basic minimum-cut method.

The authors provide theoretical justification from two perspectives: a Markov random field interpretation and sample-complexity considerations. The first connects graph partitions with probabilistic label assignments. The second examines learning in relation to the amount of data. These perspectives support the randomized method alongside its empirical evaluation.

The benefit depends on the graph’s structure. The authors explicitly note that randomization may not help when the classification problem lacks small cuts. When suitable small cuts exist, experiments show highly accurate classifiers and favorable tradeoffs between accuracy and coverage. The method also achieves good performance with a simple graph-construction procedure, making the structural condition more central than an elaborate graph-building process.
icml-2004-semi-supervised-learning-using.tldr: Randomizing graph structure improves minimum-cut semi-supervised learning in tested settings where the graph supports suitable small cuts.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems can learn from past user ratings and from descriptive attributes of users or items. This paper proposes a unified method that systematically incorporates these forms of training information into one prediction function. Its aim is to bring collaborative and content-based filtering into a common learning approach.

The key design choice is a kernel, or similarity function, between user-item pairs. Treating the pair as the object being compared allows information to generalize across both the user dimension and the item dimension. The authors also propose JRank, an online learning algorithm that generalizes perceptron learning for this formulation.

Experiments on the EachMovie dataset show significant improvements over standard approaches in the reported comparisons. These findings support the value of combining rating information with attributes through a shared similarity function. The contribution is both a representation for integrating the available information and a learning algorithm for using it, with empirical evidence from the movie recommendation setting.
icml-2004-unifying-collaborative-and-con.tldr: A similarity function over user-item pairs unifies ratings and attributes, with JRank showing improvements on EachMovie.

paragraphs: Approximate probabilistic inference often involves a tradeoff between computational speed and accuracy. Variational methods offer fast, deterministic approximations, although they are often less accurate than sampling-based MCMC methods. This paper addresses a restriction of existing variational approaches: their focus on parametric models, while MCMC methods already support the nonparametric Dirichlet process.

The authors develop a mean-field variational method for Dirichlet process inference. The approximate posterior uses a truncated stick-breaking construction, giving the approximation a finite representation of the process. This makes it possible to bring the variational approach into a setting central to Bayesian nonparametric statistics.

The method is compared with Dirichlet process samplers for Gaussian mixture models. Its motivation is particularly relevant to high-dimensional problems where sampling can be too slow to be effective. The contribution is an approximate inference route for the Dirichlet process that extends the reach of deterministic variational methods, while retaining the explicit approximation introduced by the truncated posterior construction.
icml-2004-variational-methods-for-the-di.tldr: A truncated stick-breaking posterior enables mean-field variational inference for the nonparametric Dirichlet process.

paragraphs: An AI agent’s behavior unfolds through sequences of planning, tool use, memory updates, and coordination. This position paper argues that explaining individual model predictions does not adequately account for these longer trajectories. Failures such as tool misuse, coordination breakdowns, and goal drift can involve interactions across components and escape existing audits.

The authors propose that interpretability should develop alongside agent capabilities, use methods suited to different layers of opacity, and operate throughout deployment. The emphasis is on tracing behavior over time and assigning responsibility across the system. Internal model analysis remains relevant, but it sits within a broader account of how the agent acts.

Their ATLIS framework organizes five interpretability layers across five deployment stages. It supports lightweight continuous monitoring, with deeper system-level analysis triggered by incidents according to risk. The paper presents this as a blueprint for accountable deployment: routine observation and more intensive investigation are connected within one framework for understanding agent behavior throughout its lifecycle.
icml-2026-position-accountable-deploymen.tldr: ATLIS proposes layered, lifecycle-wide interpretability for tracing agent behavior and escalating from continuous monitoring to deeper incident analysis.

paragraphs: Genomic prediction models are increasingly expected to help explain biological mechanisms. This paper argues that current evaluations of interpretability methods often rely on one method and a few persuasive examples. Such examples can make an explanation appear biologically plausible without establishing whether the method is consistently reliable or reflects the model’s actual reasoning.

A benchmark study of transcription factor binding exposes several risks. Different interpretability methods can produce conflicting explanations for the same prediction, miss known regulatory motifs, and fail to represent the model’s internal decision process faithfully. These are distinct concerns: an explanation’s agreement with another method, biological relevance, and faithfulness to the model each require attention.

The authors propose a tiered framework for systematic evaluation and reporting. Their analogy to clinical trials emphasizes rigorous design and reporting of failures alongside successes. The intended shift is toward assessing consistency, faithfulness, and biological validity across evaluations, so that isolated plausible explanations do not carry more evidential weight than they can support.
icml-2026-position-genomic-model-researc.tldr: A transcription-factor-binding benchmark motivates systematic evaluation of genomic explanations for consistency, faithfulness, and biological validity.

paragraphs: Serving language models requires deciding where requests go, when they run, and which cached information stays in memory. This position paper argues that commonly used policies, including shortest-queue routing, first-in-first-out scheduling, and least-recently-used eviction, do not adequately capture the distinctive structure of language-model inference.

The authors highlight growing key-value cache memory, differences between prompt processing and token generation, unknown output lengths, and continuous batching constraints. These characteristics interact with routing, scheduling, and memory decisions. The proposed research direction is to build mathematical models that capture those interactions and use them to design algorithms with provable performance guarantees across diverse workloads.

The paper points to emerging work combining operations research with machine-learning systems as evidence that principled methods can match or exceed heuristic performance while offering theoretical guarantees. It calls for algorithm design to become a central research topic in serving systems. This is a research agenda supported by emerging results, rather than a claim that one optimization method already resolves every serving workload.
icml-2026-position-llm-serving-needs-mat.tldr: The paper argues for LLM-specific optimization models and algorithms with performance guarantees for routing, scheduling, and cache management.

paragraphs: Generating synthetic data does not, by itself, establish a privacy claim. This position paper argues that research practice has increasingly treated synthetic origin as apparent evidence of privacy, displacing explicit statements about what an adversary could infer under specified assumptions. The authors frame this as a shift in standards of evidence within the community.

Their empirical analysis of publications across major machine-learning venues finds frequent use of synthetic data in privacy-sensitive settings without explicit threat models, inference risks, or falsifiable privacy claims. This leaves the assurance difficult to check. The paper also identifies uneven exposure, with rare and minority records facing heightened risk under such implicit assurances.

The proposed response is to make privacy assertions explicit, scoped, and open to testing and challenge. Research venues would require authors to state what privacy protection they claim and provide evidence that can be examined. The aim is to make the remaining inference risk a scientific question with accountable assumptions, rather than letting the data-generation process stand in for a privacy argument.
icml-2026-position-privacy-is-a-claim-no.tldr: The paper argues that synthetic-data privacy requires explicit, testable claims supported by evidence about inference risk.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that AI agents change the economics of cyberattacks by automating work that previously required scarce human expertise. Tailored attacks across many targets can become attractive even with small success rates. The authors contend that defenses built around the cost of manual exploitation therefore need fundamental revision.

They argue that model filtering, alignment, and output controls cannot stop adversaries who control open-weight models, bypass protections, or develop offensive capabilities independently. Their proposed response is for defenders to build offensive security intelligence in controlled settings. They treat understanding those capabilities as necessary infrastructure for anticipating adaptive attacks.

The paper recommends three coordinated actions: comprehensive benchmarks spanning the attack lifecycle, trained agents that discover real-world vulnerabilities at scale, and governance over how offensive capabilities are used and released. The governance proposal includes audited cyber ranges, releases staged by capability tier, and transferring findings into defensive-only agents. These are recommendations for developing defensive capacity responsibly, grounded in the authors’ position that agent-driven attacks are inevitable.
icml-2026-position-to-defend-against-cyb.tldr: The authors argue that controlled offensive AI research, benchmarks, and staged governance are essential to defending against agent-driven cyberattacks.

paragraphs: This position paper examines two linked problems in machine-learning peer review: managing submission volume and encouraging good reviewing behavior. The authors argue that growing participation and stronger reciprocal reviewing requirements have not resolved widespread dissatisfaction. They also call attention to the limited public discussion of what makes a review system effective.

The paper assesses existing mechanisms, offers four perspectives on popular conference practices, and proposes two alternative designs. Its central position is that meaningful improvement requires enforceable, fine-grained procedures together with incentives. General advice in reviewer guidelines is presented as insufficient to bring about the desired changes in behavior.

The proposed OpenReview Points system gives those incentives a currency-like form. Participants would earn credits through good review practices and spend them on benefits across one or more conferences, such as free registration or access to additional review resources. This is a proposal for connecting reviewing contributions to tangible privileges, making the reward structure an explicit part of peer-review design.
icml-2026-position-want-better-ml-review.tldr: The paper proposes enforceable review procedures and a credit system that rewards good reviewing with conference-related benefits.
